target.title: fix(memory): bound unsignaled remote HTTP with default timeoutMs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Memory remote HTTP (`withRemoteHttpResponse`) only forwarded an optional caller `AbortSignal`. Embedding batch / `postJson` callers often omit a signal (Google/OpenAI/Voyage upload and status polls), so a peer that accepts TCP but never returns headers could hang the Gateway forever. Idle body caps never start until headers arrive. Callers that pass a cancellation-only `AbortSignal` (no deadline) had the same hang risk when the wrapper treated any signal as a reason to skip the transport floor.

## Why This Change Was Made

Install a shared hang floor via existing `fetchWithSsrFGuard` `timeoutMs`, and compose it with any caller `AbortSignal`:

- Default: `MEMORY_REMOTE_HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s (aligned with memory remote batch budgets so large uploads are not clamped below established policy)
- Explicit `timeoutMs` override still wins
- Caller `AbortSignal` is always forwarded; `fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` compose cancellation with the floor so cancellation-only signals cannot disable the hang bound

Also forward optional `timeoutMs` through `postJson` so production JSON POST callers can override the floor without reimplementing the wrapper.

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** Unsignaled (or cancellation-only-signaled) memory remote HTTP could hang indefinitely on a stalled upstream.

**After:** Requests fail closed after 120s by default (`TimeoutError` / `request timed out`), including when a caller supplies a cancellation-only `AbortSignal`. Explicit `timeoutMs` and earlier caller aborts still win.

## Evidence

- Changed: `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/remote-http.ts`, `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/post-json.ts`
- Production path under test: `withRemoteHttpResponse` (shared by `postJson` / batch-upload / provider embedding batches) against a real local `node:http` server that never writes headers
- Regression: `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/remote-http.test.ts`, `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/post-json.test.ts`

### Caller-path hang proof (Vitest)


target.title: fix(security): bound mcporter registry read in audit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readGlobalMcporterRegistrySummary` in `src/security/audit.ts` read the global MCP registry (`stateDir/skills/config/mcporter.json`) with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, so a maliciously large or corrupted registry could exhaust memory during a security audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced the unbounded read with `readRegularFile`, which rejects symlinks and non-files and supports a byte cap. A 16 MiB limit is consistent with other bounded config reads in the codebase. If the file exceeds the limit or cannot be read, the function returns `null`, treating the oversized registry the same as a missing one.

## User Impact

Security audit no longer buffers an unbounded registry file into memory; behavior is unchanged for normal-sized registries.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a `16 MiB + 1` byte `mcporter.json` and asserts the `tools.exec.agent_skill_mcp_boundary_drift` finding is not emitted.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/security/audit-config-basics.test.ts --run` passes (8/8 tests).

target.title: fix: gateway kill leaves Codex tool processes running
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators killing an active Gateway session could still have shell or tool subprocesses continue running after the session was reported as stopped. This could leave background work consuming resources or producing side effects without an owning session.

## Why This Change Was Made

Gateway hard cancellation now closes the run spawn scope, interrupts the owned Codex turn, terminates exact-thread background terminals, and waits for OpenClaw-managed plus local Codex app-server process trees before releasing run ownership. POSIX process groups and the Windows taskkill /T fallback remain platform-specific containment boundaries; unrelated sessions are not swept.

## User Impact

After an operator kills a Gateway session, the shell and tool work owned by that run is terminated before the run is finalized. Other sessions and their processes remain unaffected.

## Evidence

- focused cancellation suite passed: 10 test files and 245 tests
- production graph, core test graph, and extension test graph typechecks passed after rebasing
- targeted oxlint and git diff --check passed
- live ACP cancellation conformance passed 3/3 on macOS; the completion marker remained absent after kill
- CI preflight, security-fast, OpenGrep, Real behavior proof, dependency guard, and initial CodeQL process-boundary shards passed on the current PR series
- max-lines ratchet passes after rebasing onto the upstream baseline fix

Known proof boundary: live Windows Job Object containment was not exercised; the Windows taskkill /T fallback is covered by regression tests.

AI-assisted: yes.

target.title: fix(line): keep group history recorded during a mention turn
target.body:
Closes #107363

## What Problem This Solves

In a LINE group with `requireMention`, ambient (unmentioned) messages are buffered as context for the next mention turn. That buffer was cleared with a **whole-key delete** after each mention turn. Webhook dispatch is fire-and-forget, so a plain message sent while the agent is still handling a mention gets recorded mid-turn — and the post-turn clear then wipes the whole window, silently dropping that message from the next turn's context. In a busy group this loses ambient context on every answered turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

`handleMessageEvent` snapshots the history window (a copy), `await`s the agent, then clears the whole key. The unmentioned-record path runs on a concurrent dispatch, so a message recorded during the `await` is lost.

The fix reads the window and captures the identity keys it consumes in **one synchronous step** (`snapshotLineGroupHistory`), passes the materialized `inboundHistory` into `buildLineMessageContext` (which no longer touches the live map), and clears **only those keys** after the turn. Because the consumed set is derived from the exact entries the turn read, an entry is either in the turn's context and cleared afterwards, or recorded later and retained — there is no boundary where both can be true.

That single read boundary matters: an earlier revision captured the keys before media download and context construction, and a message arriving in that window would have been included in the turn's `InboundHistory` yet retained by cleanup — duplicated context on the next turn. The review round caught this; the snapshot and the context read are now the same operation.

The unmentioned-record path stamps the LINE message id so entries have a stable identity (with a `timestamp/sender/body` fallback). Cleanup stays **after** the turn, so a failed turn still leaves history intact for the retry — the failure semantics are unchanged.

The snapshot/clear helpers live in `group-history.ts` (next to `group-keys.ts` / `group-policy.ts`), mirroring how Telegram keeps its group-history retention in its own module; `bot-handlers.ts` (a size-capped file) calls them and stays net-negative.

**Distinct from #101316** (per-user in-flight guard in `monitor.ts` / `in-flight-feedback.ts`, which governs concurrent-message *admission*): this PR is about the group history window's post-turn *cleanup* — a different mechanism in a different file.

## User Impact

Busy `requireMention` groups keep ambient messages that arrive while the bot is answering a mention, so the next turn sees the full recent context instead of a wiped window — and never sees an already-consumed message twice. No change for non-group chats or when there is no concurrency. A failed mention turn still preserves history for retry (unchanged).

## Evidence

### Red↔green

Degrading the helper back to a whole-key clear (the original behavior) fails the concurrency e2e and the helper's retention test. Reverting the snapshot to the earlier placement (keys captured before media download and context construction) fails the two new boundary assertions:

```
 × keeps a group message recorded during a mention turn instead of clearing it
 × keeps a message arriving between the history snapshot and context construction for the next mention
      Tests  2 failed | 29 passed (31)
```

With the fix restored, the full LINE extension suite is green:

```
 Test Files  27 passed (27)
      Tests  327 passed | 1 skipped (328)
```

### Tests

```
group-history.test.ts (helper unit):
 ✓ snapshotLineGroupHistory > reads the window and captures the identity keys of exactly the read entries
 ✓ snapshotLineGroupHistory > consumes only the entries inside the window limit
 ✓ snapshotLineGroupHistory > returns an empty snapshot without a map, key, or positive limit
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > keeps entries recorded after the snapshot and drops the consumed ones
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > deletes the key when every entry was consumed
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > no-ops without consumed keys
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > falls back to timestamp/sender/body identity when messageId is absent

bot-handlers.test.ts (concurrency e2e):
 ✓ keeps a group message recorded during a mention turn instead of clearing it
   (also asserts the turn's context received exactly the pre-mention window)
 ✓ keeps a message arriving between the history snapshot and context construction for the next mention
   (parks the turn inside context construction, records an ambient message mid-window, asserts it stays
    out of that turn's context, survives cleanup, and is consumed exactly once by the next mention)
 ✓ keeps group history intact when a mention turn fails, so the retry still has context

bot-message-context.test.ts:
 ✓ passes the caller-provided inbound history through to the context payload
```

### Live behavior proof (real LINE `requireMention` group)

Run from this branch on a real LINE channel (gateway + ngrok webhook, default `requireMention`, ids redacted). Gateway verbose log timeline:

```
00:26:13 line: skipping group message (requireMention, not mentioned)   <- ambient: "Otter says the picnic moved to Sunday"
00:26:16 line: skipping group message (requireMention, not mentioned)   <- ambient chatter
00:26:26 line: skipping group message (requireMention, not mentioned)   <- ambient chatter
00:26:32 line inbound: from=line:group:C...7c6 "...@openclaw please summarize what everyone discussed recently"
00:27:12 line: skipping group message (requireMention, not mentioned)   <- ambient MID-TURN: "Correction: it is Monday, not Sunday"
00:27:22 [line] embedded run agent end: isError=false                   <- turn 1 replies; identity-based cleanup runs
00:28:11 line inbound: from=line:group:C...7c6 "...@openclaw did anyone correct the picnic day? which day is it now?"
00:28:24 [line] embedded run agent end: isError=false                   <- turn 2 replies
```

Agent replies (from the agent session transcript, `transcript_events`):

- **Turn 1** (the correction arrived while this turn was running): *"I can see … I only have access to the **last 3 messages** in the history provided … The picnic has been moved to **Sunday**"* — the mid-turn correction is not in this turn's context; it arrived after the snapshot.
- **Turn 2**: *"Yes, there was a correction: **The picnic is now Monday**, not Sunday. Someone corrected it in the most recent message."* — the mid-turn ambient message survived the post-turn cleanup and reached the next mention exactly once. With the whole-key clear on `main`, turn 1's cleanup wipes this message and turn 2 cannot know about it.

Environment note: current `main` rejects every LINE inbound agent turn with `GatewayDrainingError` (the post-ack fire-and-forget webhook dispatch inherits the released HTTP work admission; regression window opened Jul 12). The live run needed a 3-line local admission patch — `src/process/gateway-work-admission.ts` only, unrelated to this PR's diff and not part of it. A separate report with a deterministic repro is being prepared.

### Static checks

```
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions          -> exit 0   (prod typecheck)
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions:test     -> exit 0   (test typecheck)
$ pnpm lint:extensions          -> exit 0   (oxlint)
$ oxfmt --check <touched files> -> All matched files use the correct format.
$ node scripts/check-max-lines-ratchet.mjs --base origin/main
  max-lines ratchet OK: 1231 grandfathered suppressions.
```

`bot-handlers.ts` stays net-negative; the snapshot/clear logic lives in `group-history.ts`. Merged with current `main`.

target.title: fix(ui): add min-height:0 to flex scroll containers for Firefox
target.body:
## Summary

Firefox enforces CSS Flexbox automatic minimum size more strictly than Chromium, preventing `.sidebar-content` and `.md-preview-dialog__body` from shrinking below their content height and blocking `overflow: auto` from creating a scrollable area.

- Problem: Flex children with `flex: 1` and `overflow: auto` cannot shrink below intrinsic content height in Firefox because the default `min-height: auto` computes to the content size, clipping overflow instead of scrolling.
- Solution: Add `min-height: 0` to both flex children so Firefox allows them to shrink below content height and become the inner scroll container.
- What changed:
  - `ui/src/styles/chat/sidebar.css` — `.sidebar-content` gains `min-height: 0`
  - `ui/src/styles/components.css` — `.md-preview-dialog__body` gains `min-height: 0`
- What did NOT change: No flex ancestor rules, no JS/TS logic, no layout changes in Chromium/WebKit (they already treat `min-height: 0` as the implicit flex behavior).

## Change Type & Scope

### Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

### Scope

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations

target.title: feat: add readiness conditions and providers
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, but readiness is evaluated by a fixed set of Gateway checks. Hosts and operators cannot select the additional criteria that define readiness for a deployment, plugins cannot contribute bounded observational evidence, and CLI, health, and status surfaces do not share one canonical result.

That leaves Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and other hosts maintaining private scripts to answer a basic question: is this OpenClaw instance ready to accept work under its configured requirements?

## Proposal

This draft implements the readiness portion of RFC 0018:

- normalize Gateway startup, admission, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, event-loop, configuration, plugin, and workspace evidence into structured conditions
- distinguish required conditions, which fail readiness on `False` or `Unknown`, from advisory conditions, which remain visible without changing the ready result
- let operators select built-in and plugin-contributed criteria directly with `gateway.readiness`
- let activated plugins register namespaced, self-describing criteria through the public plugin registry
- bound plugin checks with per-criterion timeouts, an overall readiness deadline, stable redacted timeout/error results, short caching, and in-flight coalescing that never duplicates a callback still pending after timeout
- return a required `ReadinessEvaluationComplete=Unknown` condition if canonical evaluation times out or fails, rather than hanging or rejecting health/status requests
- project the same canonical result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, Gateway `ready`, health, status, and `openclaw ready`
- provide human-readable and `--json` CLI output with fail-closed exit status

Example operator selection:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: ["openclaw.workspace-writable", "plugin.example.dependency"],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

Core selector IDs are configuration identities: selecting `openclaw.workspace-writable` emits the stable canonical `WorkspaceWritable` condition. Plugin criteria use their full namespaced ID as the condition type.

A plugin may contribute observational evidence without changing readiness by default:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "dependency",
  description: "Example dependency is reachable",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    const reachable = await probeDependency(pluginConfig, { signal });
    return reachable
      ? { status: "True", reason: "DependencyReachable", message: "Dependency is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "DependencyUnavailable", message: "Dependency is unavailable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes that registration as `plugin.<plugin-id>.dependency`. Operators explicitly select it in `requiredCriteria` when it belongs in their serving contract.

## Compatibility

Existing `/ready` and `/readyz` routes retain their HTTP contract: `200` when all required conditions are true and `503` otherwise. Existing installations need no readiness configuration. The universal Gateway lifecycle baseline always applies; explicitly selected criteria add deployment-specific evidence.

This PR does **not** add hosting profiles, profile selection, node-mode profiles, runtime activation identity, release conformance, Lobster concepts, tenant concepts, OCC resources, or policy/Doctor dependencies. Standard Hosting Profiles are separated into RFC 0023 so this readiness facility can stand on its own.

## Review Stack

This is one upstream PR with four commits. The fork PRs preserve the same smaller review boundaries:

- [PR 17: canonical Gateway readiness conditions](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17)
- [PR 22: workspace writability criterion](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22)
- [PR 23: selectable readiness providers](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23)
- [PR 27: canonical `openclaw ready` CLI](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27)

The implementation is rebased onto OpenClaw main `5fc7ba6da031`.

## Validation

- exact head: `89d8607aab9f9a942d45a6910cba1db3a210e239`
- all 19 changed test files pass in every selected Vitest project: 22 files/shards and 259 assertions
- Oxfmt passes on 59 changed TypeScript/JavaScript/Markdown files; Oxlint passes on 54 changed TypeScript/JavaScript files; `git diff --check` passes
- plugin SDK surface validation passes at the exact post-harvest budget: 328 public entrypoints and 10,615 public exports, with no forbidden package subpaths
- package build, public SDK declaration graph, package inventory, and tarball integrity checks pass
- final Codex review against current base reports no actionable correctness regression
- exact-head package-installed Docker proof passes with image `sha256:8add3c4f8ce2f1a444a735c43f19eac4ee0212778123fb883ff8f9f785a9fd0d`
- `/ready` and `/readyz` transition `200 -> 503 -> 200` when a required workspace is removed and restored; `/healthz` remains `200`; `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same `WorkspaceWritable / WorkspaceMissing` condition

`pnpm check:changed` is not claimed locally: this linked WSL worktree delegates that command to Blacksmith Testbox, and the local credential cannot access the `openclaw` organization. The changed-file tests and local static/package gates above passed; GitHub CI remains authoritative for repository-wide lanes.

## Published Upgrade Proof

The repository's `published-upgrade-survivor` Docker lane passed from the current published `openclaw@2026.7.1` package to a `2026.7.2` tarball carrying this four-commit readiness patch.

```text
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_PUBLISHED_BASELINE=1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_BASELINE_SPEC=openclaw@2026.7.1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_CANDIDATE=current \
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=16384 \
  bash scripts/e2e/upgrade-survivor-docker.sh
```

The lane installed and configured 2026.7.1 first, seeded agents, sessions, workspaces, credentials, channel/plugin settings, and legacy plugin dependency state, validated the baseline, upgraded the same installation through `openclaw update`, ran non-interactive Doctor and config validation, and revalidated preserved state before starting the candidate Gateway.

All 54 recorded phases passed on proved head `e5f5e97332e5495e65c1993dba258109849bdece`. Gateway startup took 47 seconds, `/healthz` 1 second, `/readyz` 1 second, and RPC status 2 seconds. The final head is a patch-equivalent rebase over seven later upstream commits; `git range-diff` shows the readiness commits unchanged except for the SDK export budget adapting to upstream's deletion. The exact final head then passed the package build, tarball integrity, and package-installed `200 -> 503 -> 200` runtime proof above.

Compatibility is explicit: the upgraded existing installation did not silently acquire `WorkspaceWritable` or another opt-in criterion as a new requirement. Its existing Gateway lifecycle baseline remained ready. An operator who explicitly requires workspace writability receives the intended fail-closed transition and matching CLI exit status.

target.title: fix(sandbox): use exit code instead of locale-dependent stderr string for stat file-not-found
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `SandboxFsBridgeImpl.stat()` at `fs-bridge.ts:211` uses `stderr.includes("No such file or directory")` to detect ENOENT. Under non-English system locales (e.g., zh_CN.UTF-8), stat(1) emits localized error messages (e.g., `没有那个文件或目录`), causing ENOENT to be missed and an Error thrown instead of returning `null`.

**Solution**: Two changes for locale-independent ENOENT detection: (1) `buildStatPlan()` — added `export LC_ALL=C` and switched to command substitution stderr capture with case pattern matching, returning exit code 2 with "ENOENT" stdout sentinel for file-not-found; (2) `fs-bridge.ts` — check `result.code === 2` + stdout "ENOENT" instead of locale-dependent stderr matching. Non-ENOENT failures (permission errors, I/O errors) still throw as before.

**What changed**: `fs-bridge-shell-command-plans.ts` +24/-2 (enhanced shell script with LC_ALL=C + sentinel), `fs-bridge.ts` +9/-3 (sentinel-based ENOENT detection), `fs-bridge.anchored-ops.test.ts` +64 (2 new locale-independence test cases).

**Design note**: The original approach used a temporary file (mktemp) to capture stderr, which added a writable temporary-directory requirement to every sandbox stat call. The current fix uses shell command substitution (`err=$(stat ... 2>&1 >/dev/null)`) instead, removing the mktemp dependency entirely.

Fixes #106780

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Sandbox stat() detection of file-not-found (ENOENT) was locale-dependent, failing on non-English systems.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic, bash 5.2.21, zh_CN.UTF-8 (non-English locale).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: See attached verify.log at docs/.local/issue-106780/verify.log (5 scenarios covering bug reproduction, LC_ALL=C fix, ENOENT sentinel, Permission denied, and normal stat)

**After-fix evidence**: Full terminal output collected on zh_CN.UTF-8 system (Chinese locale):

```

SCENARIO 1: Bug reproduction (zh_CN.UTF-8 locale)
$ stat -c "%F|%s|%y" -- /tmp/pr-evidence/nofile 2>&1
stat: 对 '/tmp/pr-evidence/nofile' 调用 statx 失败: 没有那个文件或目录
exit=1
-> Chinese stderr — .includes("No such file or directory") would MISS

SCENARIO 2: LC_ALL=C forces English stderr
$ LC_ALL=C stat -c "%F|%s|%y" -- /tmp/pr-evidence/nofile 2>&1
stat: cannot statx '/tmp/pr-evidence/nofile': No such file or directory
exit=1
-> English stderr — case pattern matches correctly

SCENARIO 3a: buildStatPlan ENOENT sentinel (target missing, parent exists)
ENOENT
exit=2 (ENOENT sentinel)

SCENARIO 3b: buildStatPlan ENOENT sentinel (parent also missing)
ENOENT
exit=2 (ENOENT sentinel)

SCENARIO 4: Permission denied (non-ENOENT error preserved)
stderr=stat: cannot statx 'restricted/data.txt': Permission denied
exit=1 (error NOT swallowed)

SCENARIO 5: Existing file stat (normal operation)
result=regular file|12|2026-07-15 13:48:40.847307706 +0800
exit=0 (success)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: zh_CN.UTF-8 — ENOENT sentinel returns null. English/POSIX locale — same. Permission errors still throw. Normal stat returns typed result unchanged. All 12 sandbox fs-bridge tests pass.

**What was not tested**: Docker containerized sandbox backend (tested with local shell using identical buildStatPlan() script). macOS/BSD (Linux 6.17.0-35 only).

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

```
 ✓ |agents-core| ../../src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.anchored-ops.test.ts (12 tests, 0 failed)
```

Key test scenarios: "returns null on stat ENOENT sentinel (locale-independent)" — mock returns exit code 2 with stdout ENOENT → bridge returns null; "throws on non-zero exit code without ENOENT sentinel" — mock returns exit code 1 with permission error → bridge throws; "stat anchors parent + basename" — verifies correct canonical-parent anchoring. All 12 tests pass.

### TypeScript

```
npx tsc --noEmit — zero errors
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(session): persist fresh usage snapshot instead of stale totalTokens fallback
target.body:
## Summary

- **Problem**: The fallback in `updateSessionStoreAfterAgentRun` used cumulative multi-call `usage` (input + cacheRead + cacheWrite) as the fresh context snapshot when `deriveSessionTotalTokens()` returned undefined. This persisted inflated values from aggregate multi-turn data rather than the final single-call's data, causing incorrect `/status` percentages and session-state decisions.

- **Solution**: Use `lastCallUsage` (the final call's usage) instead of cumulative `usage` for the fresh context snapshot fallback. When `lastCallUsage` is unavailable (no per-call data from the provider), `totalTokens` stays `undefined` (safe fallback) rather than falling through to a stale or inflated value.

- **What changed**: One line in `session-store.ts:253`: `input + (usage.cacheRead ?? 0) + (usage.cacheWrite ?? 0)` -> `(lastCallUsage?.input ?? 0) + (lastCallUsage?.cacheRead ?? 0) + (lastCallUsage?.cacheWrite ?? 0)`. Also reverted the test expectation back to `undefined`/`false` (cumulative-only CLI scenario should not produce a fresh snapshot).

- **What did NOT change**: No external API, no config, no Gateway behavior, no schema. All existing branch behavior for compaction snapshots, valid `deriveSessionTotalTokens` results, and lastCallUsage-based context is preserved.

Fixes #107324

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: When `deriveSessionTotalTokens()` returns undefined (CLI cumulative usage where per-turn tokens can't be derived) and no compaction snapshot is available, the else branch must use the final call's usage data (`lastCallUsage`) instead of the cumulative aggregate (`usage`) for the fresh context snapshot. Using cumulative data produced inflated values (e.g. 3.8M tokens from multi-turn aggregate) misleading `/status` consumers about real per-turn context window usage. This is the P1 finding from ClawSweeper review requiring "final-call-versus-cumulative" defect correction.

target.title: fix(gateway): don't retire parent Codex binding when creating a detached dashboard child
target.body:
Fixes #106778

## What Problem This Solves

Creating a dashboard child from an active Codex-backed channel session (Control UI → new dashboard chat — an ordinary child creation, not a fork) succeeds but **retires the parent session's Codex binding**, even though the parent remains the channel's current session. The next inbound parent turn then fails permanently with `Codex binding generation was retired`, recoverable only by manual SQLite surgery.

Root-cause chain (all on current `main`):
1. `createGatewaySession` emits a terminal `session_end(reason:"new")` on the **parent** for any parent-linked child when `emitCommandHooks === true` — `src/gateway/session-create-service.ts`.
2. The Codex extension treats `"new"` as terminal (`ENDED_SESSION_REASONS`) and its `session_end` handler calls `bindingStore.retireSessionGeneration()` — `extensions/codex/index.ts:48,274`.
3. The next lease attempt observes the retired generation and throws `Codex binding generation was retired`.

A detached dashboard child (its own `agent:<id>:dashboard:*` key) runs **in parallel** — it does not replace the parent as the channel's current session, so emitting a terminal `session_end` on the parent is wrong.

## Approach

The parent rolls over — terminal `session_end` on the parent, `session_start` on the child — only when the child **succeeds** it. That disposition cannot be inferred from the child's key shape: the server keeps no current-session pointer, so a key namespace cannot prove succession (the earlier `startsWith("dashboard:")` gate was a heuristic). The caller declares it explicitly via a new optional `succeedsParent` flag on `sessions.create`; the gate reads the flag:

```ts
const childSucceedsParent = params.fork !== true && params.succeedsParent === true;
```

The namespace invariant is enforced by a **loud boundary validation** rather than silent inference: `succeedsParent` requires an explicit non-dashboard successor key and conflicts with `fork`; a keyless/minted or dashboard-namespaced child (auto-managed, detached) is rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST`. A mis-declared succession therefore fails loudly instead of silently retiring a still-active parent's binding.

- **Only TUI `/new`** (an explicit `tui-*` successor) declares `succeedsParent: true` — it still emits the parent `session_end` + child `session_start`.
- **Every other create path** — minted dashboard child (webchat "new chat"), fork, catalog/work child — is parallel by default and unchanged: no parent `session_end`, child `session_start` fires.
- **Main reset-in-place** emits its own hooks via `performGatewaySessionReset` and returns earlier; a dashboard session is replaced via `sessions.reset` (which retires its binding in place), never a create-succession.
- The parent's `before_reset` / `command:new` hooks (documented Control UI behavior, #76957) are untouched.

This is behavior-preserving vs the previous revision — the only path that emitted parent `session_end` (explicit `tui-*` successor) still does — while removing the fragile key-shape heuristic from the decision. Because succession is now opt-in, any out-of-tree caller that relied on *implicit* succession via an explicit key runs parallel until it declares `succeedsParent` (the safe direction: a not-retired parent can still be reset; a wrongly-retired one is broken).

**Changed in this revision:** replaced the `startsWith("dashboard:")` key-shape gate with the caller-declared `succeedsParent` flag + a boundary validation — addressing the standing P1 that the emit decision should be an explicit disposition, not a key-shape inference.

**Maintainer note.** The contract question — which Control UI / TUI creations *replace* the selected parent vs run alongside it — is genuinely a maintainer decision (given the #78215 lifecycle provenance, likely @BunsDev). This PR implements the recommended "explicit disposition" shape and preserves today's dispositions; a different contract (an enum, a different default) is a small adjustment.

Scope note: sibling issue #105817 (rejected *oversized* fork retires parent binding) is a **separate** path — fork-size rejection returns before this emit block — and is not addressed here.

## Evidence

### Persisted-state consequence — proven in-boundary over a real store

The destructive step lives in the Codex extension, and its bundled suite already asserts it over a **real** `createCodexAppServerBindingStore`: `session_end(reason:"new")` retires the generation (`read() → undefined` — the `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` tombstone #106778 reports), while non-terminal reasons (`shutdown`, `restart`, `compaction`) leave it intact. So the persisted mutation is real and reason-selective — suppressing the parent `session_end` for a parallel child is exactly what keeps the binding alive.

### Gate A/B + validation (real gateway session-create path, deterministic)

`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` toggles only the disposition:

```
explicit tui-* successor (succeedsParent)        → parent session_end(reason:"new") + child session_start
minted dashboard child (default)                 → no parent session_end; child session_start
fork                                             → no parent session_end
succeedsParent + {dashboard-keyed|keyless|fork}  → INVALID_REQUEST (no hooks)
```

- **65** focused lifecycle tests (`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` + `server.sessions.create.test.ts`) + **147** TUI tests pass (Node 25.9.0).
- **Static**: `tsgo:core` / `tsgo:core:test` clean.
- **Preservation**: `extensions/codex/` unchanged — a genuine `session_end reason:"new"` still retires the binding.

A full Codex app-server E2E completing model turns needs OpenAI auth unavailable in CI, but the model turn is orthogonal to this fix — the fix is precisely about *not* retiring the parent, which the gate + the in-boundary retirement suite together establish.

## Tests

`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` (explicit `tui-*` successor with `succeedsParent` → parent `session_end` + child `session_start`; detached dashboard child → no parent `session_end`, child `session_start`; reset-in-place + `command:new`/`before_reset` unchanged; **new** — `succeedsParent` + dashboard-keyed child, keyless child, and fork each → `INVALID_REQUEST`), `server.sessions.create.test.ts` (selected-global dashboard child and fork → no parent `session_end`), `tui-command-handlers.test.ts` (`/new` declares `succeedsParent: true`).

target.title: fix(mcp): isolate per-server failures so healthy MCP tools still materialize
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #106665

When one MCP server fails to connect or crashes during catalog materialization, the uncaught error propagates through `runTasksWithConcurrency` → `firstError` → `dispose ALL sessions` → throw to agent run setup. This kills the entire agent bundle runtime — healthy MCP server tools are lost along with the broken one.

#### Why This Change Was Made

The existing per-server task's `try/catch` started at `ensureSessionConnected` (line 646), leaving session creation, `Client` construction, and map operations unprotected. Any error before the `try` escaped through `runTasksWithConcurrency`'s `firstError` mechanism.

This moves the `try` boundary to cover the full per-server task lifecycle, hoists `session` and `reusedSession` declarations outside the `try`, and adds `failIfDisposed()` re-throw inside the `catch` so disposal still propagates. External failures (network, crash, protocol errors) become `McpToolCatalogDiagnostic` entries without affecting healthy servers.

#### User Impact

No visible impact under normal operation. When an MCP server fails, the agent run continues with available tools from healthy servers instead of aborting entirely.

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` core passes
- **Lint:** `oxlint` clean
- **Tests:** `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts` — 74 tests (+1: `isolates a broken MCP server so healthy servers still materialize tools`)
- **Change scope:** 2 files, +67 −16 lines
  - `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.ts` — move `try/catch` boundary up to cover full per-server lifecycle
  - `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts` — new test with real MCP subprocess (healthy + `process.exit(1)` broken)
  - No config, CLI, SDK, docs surface affected

- **Live standalone proof — real MCP processes:**

```

Catalog Result:

✓ healthy server in catalog
```

target.title: feat(tui): opt-in persistence and agent visibility for `!`/`!!` local shell commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

TUI-local `!`-prefixed shell commands render a live local echo but are never persisted: closing the TUI loses them, session resume never shows them, and the agent cannot see what the operator ran or what it printed — even though the `BashExecutionMessage`/`excludeFromContext` data model and the LLM-context filtering for it already exist in `packages/agent-core` (previously unused by any production code path).

Split out of #103147 per review feedback there; that PR now carries only the rendering fixes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Operators often run a `!` command specifically to show the agent something (Claude Code's own `!` behaves this way). But local shell output can also be sensitive, so persistence and model visibility must be a deliberate choice, not a silent default:

- The session consent prompt now offers **No** / **Yes, local only** / **Yes, and share with the agent**. **Local only is the shipped, pre-existing behavior and stays the default expectation** — nothing is saved or shared unless the operator explicitly picks the share option.
- With sharing enabled, `!cmd` persists agent-visible (the agent sees it on its next turn) and `!!cmd` persists history-only (`excludeFromContext: true`, never reaches the model). Both semantics are stated in the consent prompt itself.

Implementation: an additive, hidden (`advertise: false`, `operator.admin`) `chat.injectBashExecution` gateway RPC modeled on `chat.inject`, implemented in both TUI backends (embedded calls the shared core directly in-process; gateway goes over the RPC). No live broadcast: the originating client already rendered its own local echo. History replay renders `bashExecution` entries on session resume.

Two defects found during review/testing are fixed here as well:

- A failed spawn emits both `error` and `close`; a shared settled-guard ensures one command persists at most once.
- Rows injected while an agent run is in flight now carry `appendMode: "side"` (like `chat.inject`'s assistant bookkeeping rows) so they do not steal the run's active leaf. Without this, persisting a `!` result mid-run tripped the embedded runner's session-file fence ("session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released") and killed the run. The run adopts side entries into the chain on its next append, so the agent still sees them next turn.

## User Impact

- Default behavior is unchanged: `!` commands stay local-only unless the operator opts into sharing at the consent prompt.
- With sharing enabled, `!` output survives session resume and is visible to the agent next turn; `!!` output survives resume but never reaches the model.
- Running a shared `!` command while the agent is mid-turn no longer kills the run with a session takeover error.

## Evidence

- `src/tui/tui-local-shell.test.ts` — 12 tests: consent options (local-only default persists nothing; share option persists), `!` vs `!!` `excludeFromContext` round-trip, no-scope/no-backend skips, persistence-failure surfacing, once-only persistence on error-then-close, plus the pre-existing output-cap/UTF-16/cwd guards.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.inject-bash-execution.test.ts` — parentId chain preserved, `excludeFromContext` round-trip, **mid-run side-append regression test** (fence takeover repro), idle active-append, unresolved-identity failure.
- `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`, `src/tui/embedded-backend.test.ts` — both backend implementations (RPC params/result shapes; embedded in-process delegation and failure surfacing).
- `src/gateway/server-methods-list.test.ts` — hidden method not advertised, handler dispatchable.
- Full `src/tui` suite green locally; protocol schema regenerated (`pnpm protocol:gen` / `protocol:gen:swift` — Swift models committed).
- **Live gateway-backed evidence** (real gateway, real model, no mocks): consent gate, `!`/`!!` visibility split, restart replay, same-key cross-agent isolation, and storage-level `excludeFromContext` verification — https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/103648#issuecomment-4967407562 (recorded on head `7a293b5c35`; later heads carry the LOC-ratchet modularization, proof-artifact cleanup, and consent-wording update — no feature-path behavior change).

target.title: fix(mattermost): backfill thread history from server when in-memory window is empty
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Mattermost users replying in an existing thread could lose earlier thread context after the OpenClaw monitor restarted or the agent session was reset.

Fixes #93204

## Why This Change Was Made

The Mattermost monitor now backfills a cold local thread-history window from the Mattermost thread endpoint after inbound admission gates pass. The backfill marker is keyed by the stored thread `sessionId`, not the stable route session key, so a real `/new` or session reset in a thread gets its own recovery fetch while same-session follow-ups avoid repeated server fetches.

When the first cold turn has no stored thread session entry yet, the monitor records a pending backfill marker and adopts it once `recordInboundSessionMeta` creates the stored session id. That keeps the marker stable for same-session follow-ups and failed-fetch no-retry, without blocking a later real session-id rotation.

Recovery is now bounded on three axes flagged in review:

- **Thread response size.** `fetchMattermostThreadPosts` requests only the newest `historyLimit + 1` posts via `?perPage=<limit>&direction=up`, then restores ascending chronological order. `GET /posts/{id}/thread` returns the entire thread at the Mattermost default (`perPage=0`), so an unbounded thread would otherwise allocate and parse on the inbound path. The endpoint reads camelCase `perPage` (not `per_page`), so the limit is actually applied.
- **Marker lifecycle.** Backfill tracking uses one marker per thread history key (`Map<historyKey, sessionId>`) instead of a process-lifetime `Set` of `historyKey:session` compound keys. A plugin-local 1000-key LRU cap (`evictOldThreadBackfillMarkers`, matching the `channelHistories` window size) keeps the marker map from outgrowing the history window it accompanies; the cap stays in the plugin rather than touching core history internals. An evicted thread simply re-backfills on its next cold inbound turn. The stored session id is read only after the admission gates, so dropped pre-admission posts never touch the session store.
- **Concurrent cold turns.** Under the default zero-debounce config, two first cold-thread messages can overlap on the awaited thread-history fetch. The first turn sets the completed-attempt marker and publishes a per-history-key in-flight promise; an overlapping same-session turn now awaits that one bounded fetch instead of seeing the marker and skipping into a context-free reply. The in-flight handle is cleared once the fetch settles, so afterward the marker alone governs the intentional one-attempt-per-session no-retry.

## User Impact

Mattermost thread replies keep useful prior context after restart or `/new`, without repeated thread-history requests, unbounded thread fetches, or unbounded per-session marker growth on long-lived monitors. Concurrent first cold-thread messages under zero-debounce no longer race into a context-free reply.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/client.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts`: **3 files, 115 passed**. Covers stored thread `sessionId` rotation, same-session no-refetch, failed-fetch no-retry, dropped pre-admission posts, adopt-pending-marker without blocking later rotation, the initially-missing session entry path, marker-map eviction, and the new concurrent-turn deferred-fetch case.
- `oxlint` (repo binary) on the changed prod + test files: **passed**. `tsgo --noEmit -p extensions/mattermost/tsconfig.json`: **passed**.

target.title: fix(ui): add timeout to control-ui bootstrap config fetch
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `loadApplicationConfig` in the Control-UI bootstrap does not set a deadline on its config endpoint fetch. If the server stops responding, the retry loop over auth candidates hangs indefinitely for each attempt, blocking the entire UI startup.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to the config endpoint `fetch()` call. When the server does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects with a `TimeoutError`, the caller's `try/catch` returns `null`, and the UI proceeds without the server-provided config (gracefully falling back to defaults).

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `CONFIG_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to the existing `fetch()` call in `ui/src/app/config.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to a background bootstrap fetch. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Failure path (timeout → catch → return null) already exists for other errors.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Stalled config endpoint fetch now aborts after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely, allowing the UI to proceed with default config. The fix follows the same AbortSignal.timeout pattern used in earlier browser screenshot fetch timeout fixes.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation, vitest with jsdom environment). The test uses fake timers for deterministic timeout verification without real wall-clock delay. The vitest framework handles the fake timer advancement automatically.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx vitest run ui/src/app/config.test.ts` — unit test covering timeout behavior (passed 2/2). The test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` to control the AbortSignal.timeout timer and a mock fetch that never resolves, verifying the deadline abort fires at exactly 15 seconds.

**After-fix evidence**: Test output confirms `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` is passed to the fetch call and a stalled fetch aborts cleanly after the deadline, returning null for graceful degradation. The verify.log recording shows the full test run with COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0.

**Observed result after the fix**: Both test cases pass — (1) signal is present on the fetch init, (2) a never-resolving fetch rejects cleanly after the deadline and the config falls back to default values. Without the fix, the same test would either deadlock (if fetch never resolves) or produce no timeout protection at all.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end Gateway test with a genuinely hanging server is not practical in CI for this type of fix. The unit tests verify the timeout contract at the function level using vitest fake timers, which is the standard approach used across the codebase for timeout behavior testing.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/app/config.test.ts` → exit 0, 2 passed
- Test 1: verifies `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` is passed to the fetch call
- Test 2: verifies a stalled fetch aborts after the deadline and falls back to default config

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal mechanism change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.title: feat(discord): opt-in Discord Activities widget support
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agents can render rich, interactive HTML widgets in the web Control UI, but Discord answers are limited to markdown, embeds, and components — there is no way to show an agent-authored HTML widget to a Discord user. Discord messages cannot embed arbitrary HTML at all, so the only supported route for real HTML-in-Discord is a Discord **Activity** (an app hosted in a sandboxed iframe inside the Discord client).

This adds an opt-in Discord Activities integration so an agent can post a widget that a user opens as an interactive Activity inside Discord.

## Why This Change Was Made

Requested capability: give the agent a way to surface interactive HTML to Discord users. The design constraints:

- **Off by default.** When `channels.discord.activities` is not configured, nothing changes — no HTTP routes, no agent tool, no interaction handler are registered. Zero new surface for existing users.
- **Easy to enable.** One config block plus documented Developer Portal + tunnel steps. When enabled, the `discord_widget` tool becomes available to agents in Discord sessions automatically (gated per account).
- **Transport-only channel.** Widget/session/token policy lives in the Discord plugin; core is untouched except for the additive config surface.

## User Impact

New, opt-in only. Once an operator configures `channels.discord.activities` (client secret + a public HTTPS route to the gateway, e.g. a Cloudflare Tunnel):

1. The agent calls `discord_widget` with self-contained HTML + a title.
2. OpenClaw stores the widget and posts a message with an **Open widget** button.
3. The user clicks it → Discord launches the OpenClaw Activity (`LAUNCH_ACTIVITY`, interaction callback type 12).
4. The Activity shell authenticates the user via Discord OAuth, checks them against the account allowlist, and renders the widget HTML in a nested sandboxed iframe.

Security model:
- OAuth identifies the Discord user before any widget metadata is returned; the user must match the account `allowFrom`/`dm.allowFrom` (open-DM accounts allow all, matching existing DM policy).
- The primary widget lookup is by an unguessable 22-char widget id carried in `custom_id` (a capability). The fallback, used only when Discord omits `custom_id`, resolves the channel from Discord's **Activity Instance API** under bot auth and verifies the requesting user is an active participant — a client-supplied channel id is never trusted.
- OAuth sessions expire after 15 minutes; widget document capabilities are single-use and expire after 60 seconds; widgets expire after 7 days (max 64 retained per plugin instance).
- Widget HTML runs under `sandbox="allow-scripts"` with a CSP that blocks all network access and external resources.
- The public token-exchange route is rate-limited per client IP, with a global budget charged only for well-formed, account-resolved exchange attempts so anonymous traffic cannot exhaust it.

Config keys (documented in `docs/channels/discord-activities`):
- `channels.discord.activities.clientSecret` — OAuth2 client secret (sensitive; falls back to `DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET`).
- `channels.discord.activities.applicationId` — optional; defaults to the bot application id learned at startup.

## Evidence

- New agent tool `discord_widget`, HTTP routes under `/discord/activity` (auth: plugin, registered only when enabled), launch-button interaction handler, OAuth token exchange, session/widget/doc-token SQLite-backed stores, and a standalone Activity shell that bundles `@discord/embedded-app-sdk`.
- Config contract updated in lockstep: exported types, zod schema (client secret registered sensitive/redacted), help/labels, UI hints, generated bundled-channel metadata, and docs baseline.
- Docs: new `docs/channels/discord-activities` setup page (Developer Portal, Cloudflare Tunnel example, security model, troubleshooting) + config-key cross-links from `docs/channels/discord`.
- Tests: colocated `extensions/discord/src/activities/*.test.ts` cover config gating, tool execute (store + button + oversized/ fragment HTML), interaction launch/auth, OAuth happy/401/403/503, per-IP + global rate limits, session/widget/doc-token single-use, the Activity-instance channel resolution + participant check, and vendor-asset serving/fallback. Plugin-state `maxValueBytes` per-namespace limit added with tests. Bundled-plugin-assets + runtime-postbuild tests cover the new SDK build hook/static asset.
- Validation: `pnpm check:changed` + full `extensions/discord`, `src/plugin-state`, and touched `src/config` suites green on Blacksmith Testbox. Live smoke against a scratch gateway with the feature configured: shell `200`, bogus code `401`, unauth widget `401`, forged instance/channel with fake session `401`, vendor SDK asset `200` serving the real bundle. Autoreview (Codex gpt-5.6-sol) clean.
- The SDK browser bundle is a gitignored build artifact produced by `scripts/build-discord-activity-sdk.mjs` (mirrors the diffs-language-pack precedent).

Live-Discord items that still need real-client confirmation (documented in-page): whether `custom_id` propagates through `LAUNCH_ACTIVITY` (the Activity-instance fallback covers the case where it does not), and Developer Portal URL-mapping behavior.

target.title: fix(shared): complete avatar MIME allowlist and add subtype validation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The avatar MIME handling has two concrete gaps:

1. **Missing `.ico` support**: `resolveAvatarMime("avatar.ico")` returns `"application/octet-stream"` instead of `"image/x-icon"`, even though `.ico` is already recognized as a valid avatar path by `AVATAR_PATH_EXT_RE` and `looksLikeAvatarPath()`. Additionally, `isSupportedLocalAvatarExtension("avatar.ico")` returns `false`, preventing `.ico` files from being used as local avatar files. `.ico` is a standard Windows favicon/icon format with the IANA-registered MIME type `image/x-icon`.

2. **No MIME subtype validation for data URLs**: `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl` only checks the `data:image/` prefix without validating the specific image subtype against an allowlist. This allows data URLs with non-standard or non-image MIME subtypes to pass validation, accepting content that is not a supported avatar format.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Added `.ico` 鈫?`"image/x-icon"` to `AVATAR_MIME_BY_EXT` and `.ico` to `LOCAL_AVATAR_EXTENSIONS` 鈥?`image/x-icon` is the IANA-registered MIME type for ICO files.
- Created explicit `AVATAR_ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES` set containing the supported image subtypes (`png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`, `svg+xml`, `x-icon`, `tiff`) and `isAllowedAvatarMimeType()` public function.
- Added `extractDataUrlMime()` helper in `avatar-limits.ts` to extract the MIME subtype from `data:image/<subtype>;...` URLs.
- Updated `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl` to validate the extracted MIME subtype against the allowlist, instead of only checking the `data:image/` prefix.

## User Impact

| Input | Before | After | Rationale |
|-------|--------|-------|-----------|
| `resolveAvatarMime("avatar.ico")` | `"application/octet-stream"` | `"image/x-icon"` | Standard IANA MIME for ICO |
| `isSupportedLocalAvatarExtension("avatar.ico")` | `false` | `true` | ICO is a valid image format |
| `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl("data:image/bmp;base64,...")` | `true` (accepted) | `false` (rejected) | BMP not in allowlist |
| `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl("data:image/png;base64,...")` | `true` | `true` | PNG is in allowlist |
| `isAllowedAvatarMimeType("image/svg+xml")` | N/A | `true` | New public function |

## Evidence / Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** (1) `.ico` files not recognized as supported avatar files despite being valid image format. (2) Data URL MIME subtype not validated, allowing non-image or unsupported image formats to pass `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl`.
- **Real environment tested:** Node.js runtime with vitest.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  npx vitest run src/shared/avatar-policy.test.ts src/shared/avatar-limits.test.ts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```
  # avatar-policy.test.ts
   鉁?avatar policy > classifies avatar URI and path helpers directly
   鉁?avatar policy > checks path containment safely
   鉁?avatar policy > detects avatar-like path strings
   鉁?avatar policy > supports expected local file extensions
   鉁?avatar policy > resolves mime type from extension
   鉁?avatar policy > isAllowedAvatarMimeType accepts registered avatar MIME types

  # avatar-limits.test.ts
   鉁?isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl > accepts the exact encoded boundary and rejects larger or non-image data URLs
   鉁?isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl > rejects unregistered image MIME subtypes in data URLs

   Test Files  2 passed (2)
        Tests  8 passed (8)
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** `resolveAvatarMime("a.ico")` returns `"image/x-icon"`. `isSupportedLocalAvatarExtension("avatar.ico")` returns `true`. `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl("data:image/bmp;base64,...")` returns `false`. All PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP/SVG data URLs continue to pass.
- **What was not tested:** Actual render pipeline integration. The fix is a pure validation gate 鈥?it rejects inputs that were previously accepted but would have failed downstream (unsupported image decoders).

## Regression Test Plan

- **Coverage level:** Unit test
- **Target test files:** `src/shared/avatar-policy.test.ts`, `src/shared/avatar-limits.test.ts`
- **Scenario locked in:** (1) `.ico` resolves to `image/x-icon` and is supported as local extension. (2) `isAllowedAvatarMimeType` accepts png/jpeg/gif/webp/svg+xml/x-icon/tiff, rejects bmp/octet-stream/plain. (3) `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl` rejects `data:image/bmp;base64,...` and `data:image/x-unknown;...`, accepts valid image MIME types. (4) Existing boundary test continues to pass.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** The tests cover both sides of the MIME allowlist (accept valid, reject invalid), the `.ico` resolution path, and the existing data URL boundary check.

## Root Cause

- **Root cause (`.ico`):** `AVATAR_MIME_BY_EXT` and `LOCAL_AVATAR_EXTENSIONS` never included `.ico`, despite it being a standard IANA-registered image format already recognized by path regex and `looksLikeAvatarPath()`.
- **Root cause (MIME allowlist):** `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl` relied solely on the `data:image/` prefix regex, performing no subtype validation. Any string starting with `data:image/` was accepted regardless of the actual image format.
- **Missing detection / guardrail:** No explicit allowlist existed for avatar image MIME subtypes.

target.title: fix: external plugin tabs fail under gateway auth
target.body:
Closes #107255

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users opening an external plugin Control UI tab would see the embedded panel fail with `401 Unauthorized` when the plugin route uses Gateway auth and the Gateway is running in token/password auth mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

External plugin tab descriptors already advertise gateway-local `path` values, and the Control UI should keep rendering those tabs as ordinary sandboxed iframes. This change issues short-lived, signed, HttpOnly plugin-tab cookies after authenticated Control UI read auth, then accepts those cookies only inside the plugin HTTP route auth stage.

The cookie handoff is now bounded in two ways:

- Browser cookie `Path` is scoped to each advertised external plugin tab path.
- The signed payload carries the same route path and the current shared Gateway auth generation, so sibling plugin routes and stale credentials are rejected before runtime scopes are derived.

Direct unauthenticated plugin route requests still return `401`, Gateway credentials are not placed in iframe URLs, and external tab rendering stays a normal `iframe src` load.

## User Impact

Operators can open external plugin Control UI tabs whose HTTP routes are protected with `auth: "gateway"` instead of making those routes public, switching to plugin-managed auth, or putting Gateway credentials in iframe URLs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-ui.http.test.ts src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts`
  - Result: `2 passed`, `129 passed`
- `git diff --check origin/main..HEAD`
  - Result: passed
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-ui-plugin-auth-cookie.ts src/gateway/control-ui.http.test.ts src/gateway/control-ui.ts src/gateway/http-auth-utils.ts src/gateway/server-http.ts src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts`
  - Result: passed
- `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=16384 npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit --pretty false`
  - Result: still fails in pre-existing unrelated `src/plugins/providers.test.ts` readonly tuple errors, not in this gateway/plugin-tab change.

Security regression coverage added:

- Accepts a route-scoped plugin-tab cookie for the matching gateway-auth plugin tab route.
- Accepts child paths under the bound route, for tab assets such as `/secure-hook/assets/app.js`.
- Rejects the cookie on sibling gateway-auth plugin routes.
- Rejects the cookie after the shared Gateway auth generation changes.
- Confirms bootstrap only emits plugin-tab cookies when visible external plugin tab paths exist, and checks `Path=/secure-hook`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite=Strict`.

AI-assisted: yes. I used Codex to inspect the Gateway plugin HTTP auth flow, tighten the signed cookie handoff in response to ClawSweeper's security review, add focused regression tests, rebase onto current `main`, and run the validation above. I understand the change: authenticated Control UI read auth mints short-lived route-scoped cookies for visible external plugin tabs, plugin-route auth accepts those cookies only for matching route/current-auth-generation requests, and runtime scopes come from the signed cookie rather than from request headers or URL credentials.

target.title: fix: check channel health after startup grace
target.body:
Closes #105668

## What Problem This Solves

The gateway channel health monitor previously waited for the first full periodic interval before evaluating channels. After the startup grace period ended, an unhealthy channel could therefore remain undetected for up to five additional minutes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Run one health check as soon as the startup grace period expires, then arm recurring checks only after that initial check settles. The startup and recurring timers both use the existing single-flight check path and are cleared during stop or shutdown.

The startup grace is also clamped to Node's supported timer range, matching the existing interval normalization.

## User Impact

Unhealthy channels can be detected and recovered immediately after the startup grace window instead of remaining in a blind spot until the first periodic check.

This PR is AI-assisted. I reviewed the implementation and understand the timer and lifecycle changes.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.test.ts` — 45 tests passed.
- Focused `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — passed.

Local validation used Node 24.14, slightly below the repository's Node 24.15 engine floor; CI remains the supported-version proof.

### Exact-head real Gateway runtime proof (`18e88af7e0c940c081214c6029a10861b8db893a`)

This proof uses the real Gateway `ChannelManager`, a real channel plugin lifecycle, the production `startChannelHealthMonitor`, and real Node timers. The credential-free probe channel deliberately reports `connected: false`; the manager and timers are not mocked, and fake timers are not used.

Related: #94279

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw update` directly inside a
container could receive host-oriented EACCES recovery guidance such as using
`sudo` or changing the npm global prefix.

Those steps are misleading inside a container because an in-container package
update is not durable across recreation.

actions. It covers direct CLI invocation of `openclaw update`.

## User Impact

Container operators who invoke the updater directly now receive recovery steps
that match the durable container deployment model instead of host package
installation advice.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound BOOT.md file read size
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadBootFile` in `src/gateway/boot.ts` read the workspace `BOOT.md` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, allowing an arbitrarily large file to be loaded into memory during gateway boot.

## Why This Change Was Made

Switch to `readRegularFile` from `../infra/regular-file.js` with a 16 MiB cap, matching the pattern used for other bounded file reads. The helper rejects non-file targets; the boot path first resolves `BOOT.md` via `fs.realpath` so a symlink pointing to a regular file is followed and read normally. An oversized `BOOT.md` is treated as empty/missing so the boot step is skipped safely instead of failing or allocating excessive memory.

## User Impact

No behavioral change for normal `BOOT.md` files. Pathologically large `BOOT.md` files are now handled safely and consistently: the boot check is skipped rather than attempting an unbounded read. Symlinks to regular files continue to work.

target.title: fix(ai): don't run repairJson on already-valid JSON
target.body:
## Summary

`parseJsonWithRepair` unconditionally ran `repairJson`, whose `looksLikeWindowsPathPrefix` heuristic cannot distinguish a real Windows drive letter (`C:`) from an ordinary `<letter>:` token (e.g. Python `with open(x) as f:`). A valid `\n` escape immediately after such a token was doubled into a literal backslash-n, corrupting multi-line script arguments in tool calls (broke exec'd Python/heredocs).

This PR parses the input as-is first and only falls back to `repairJson` when the input is genuinely malformed.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the class of bug reported in #14452 ("Files are written using literal `\n` instead of real new line breaks"): legitimate `\n`/`\t` escapes emitted by the model were being corrupted into literal backslash sequences by the repair heuristic, breaking multi-line file writes and exec'd scripts.

## Evidence

- Regression tests added in `packages/ai/src/utils/json-parse.test.ts` covering the `<letter>:` + `\n` case (a Python `with open(x) as f:\n...` payload round-trips intact).
- Commit `a7bbd8e`.

## Related issue

Related to #14452 (currently CLOSED / labeled `stale`). This PR addresses the underlying bug — consider reopening #14452 to track it.

## Open question for reviewers

The existing test `src/llm/utils/json-parse.test.ts` asserts that unescaped Windows paths like `{"path":"C:\new\file"}` are "repaired" into `C:\\new\\file`. Since that input is syntactically valid JSON, the parse-as-is-first approach now interprets `\n`/`\f` as control characters instead. These two behaviors are mutually exclusive. Which semantics should win — honoring valid JSON (fixes #14452) or preserving unescaped Windows paths? Happy to adjust the fix or update that test based on the decision.

target.body:
## Context capsule

This is PR1/5 in the clean release-head durable core replacement stack. It is docs/RFC only: it establishes the durable-core boundary, root-cause model, value proposition, and validation plan before implementation PRs claim runtime behavior.

The replacement stack is rebased onto latest `release/2026.7.1` so maintainers and ClawSweeper can review a clean topology without the old beta3 cumulative CI drift.

## Durable core stack overview

Durable core is the shared, opt-in runtime substrate that records accepted work identity, ordered steps/events, parent-child links, bounded refs, recovery states, wake/attention obligations, delivery evidence, and read-only inspection for long-running OpenClaw agent/session/task/subagent work.

It is needed because OpenClaw can accept long-running work, delegate it, defer it, route it through channels, or recover after restart without one consistent durable obligation that later code can inspect, recover, acknowledge, or fail closed. The recurring failure class includes coordinator silence, restart/interruption loss, stale running work, parent/child handoff gaps, delivery/attention uncertainty, and side-effect uncertainty.

The core sits below Task Flow, Workboard, plugins, sessions, and channel UI. Those surfaces may project from durable facts, but they should not own the persistence boundary.

Stack order:
1. PR1/5 — docs/RFC/root-cause/boundary anchor and proof plan.
2. PR2/5 — runtime foundation/core and persisted durable state invariants.
3. PR3/5 — wake targets, durable producers, replay/recovery semantics.
4. PR4/5 — controls/inspection plus CLI/Gateway integration surface.
5. PR5/5 — internal session delivery handoff for resolved session targets.

Current PR: **PR1/5 — durable runtime RFC/docs**.

## Stack position

- Stack item: PR1/5
- Current PR summary: adds the durable core architecture RFC, test/proof plan, docs map entries, and i18n glossary labels.
- Dependency/base: `openclaw/openclaw:release/2026.7.1` at `09229c7aaad60c6ed1ec3bde685f191299148776`
- This PR head: `mjnkao/openclaw:codex/openclaw-durable-release-head-pr1-rfc-20260714` at `3cb8fea1bc63ef52a5d815dfb5ec620aaade1bc6`
- Focused diff range: `09229c7aaad60c6ed1ec3bde685f191299148776..3cb8fea1bc63ef52a5d815dfb5ec620aaade1bc6`
- Downstream dependency: PR2/5 runtime core depends on this RFC/docs base.
- Supersedes: replaces earlier reviewed PR #104246 after the release branch advanced.
- Does not claim: runtime behavior, wake replay, CLI/Gateway controls, session handoff, external transport delivery, or product retry/resume policy.

## Dependency / promotion gate

- This PR should be reviewed as the PR1/5 docs/RFC slice on top of `release/2026.7.1`.
- The next PR should not be promoted until this PR reaches the agreed review threshold (`>= platinum hermit`) or maintainers explicitly waive the gate.
- If ClawSweeper asks for proof/fixes here, the stack pauses on this PR until those are addressed.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw can accept long-running work, delegate it to subagents, defer it through waits, route it through channels, and recover after restarts. Today those flows do not share one durable obligation model that later code can inspect, recover, acknowledge, or fail closed.

The repeated failure class is broader than one channel, UI, plugin, or task surface:

- coordinator silence after delegated or detached work;
- restart/interruption loss where accepted work has no inspectable recovery obligation;
- stale running sessions/tasks that are hard to distinguish from actively owned work;
- parent/child handoff gaps between sessions, subagents, and task runners;
- wake/attention uncertainty after a result or recovery signal exists;
- delivery uncertainty where internal ownership, external transport, and user-visible consumption can be conflated;
- side-effect uncertainty when retries or repairs are attempted without a durable evidence trail.

This PR defines the generic durable-core boundary and root-cause model so later implementation PRs can be reviewed against the actual failure class instead of one-off symptoms.

## User value

For OpenClaw users and operators, durable core aims to make long-running work safer and easier to trust:

- accepted work can be inspected after silence or restart;
- recovery state can be explained instead of guessed;
- duplicate retries and ghost work are easier to prevent;
- parent/child handoffs become auditable;
- operators get safer read-only inspection before repair;
- product surfaces can build higher-level workflows without each inventing its own persistence boundary.

## Why this is upstream-friendly

This PR intentionally starts with docs/RFC and proof boundaries before runtime changes. It is upstream-friendly because it:

- defines the shared core boundary before adding implementation weight;
- keeps durable core opt-in and below product-specific surfaces;
- avoids making Task Flow, Workboard, plugins, sessions, or channel UI own the persistence contract;
- separates internal durable evidence from external/user-visible delivery claims;
- gives maintainers a sequential stack with focused review slices;
- keeps migration, schema, and runtime risk deferred to implementation PRs with explicit proof gates;
- makes rollback/review boundaries clearer than a single monolithic PR.

## Scope

- Durable core architecture RFC.
- Root-cause analysis and failure taxonomy.
- Test/proof plan for later implementation PRs.
- Docs map and docs navigation updates.
- zh-CN glossary entries for new/changed doc labels.
- Stack framing and review boundaries.

## Non-scope

- No runtime behavior.
- No database/schema migration.
- No CLI/Gateway controls.
- No worker loop or wake replay implementation.
- No plugin/channel delivery behavior.
- No Task Flow or Workboard product feature implementation.

target.title: fix(ui): add AbortSignal.timeout to nostr profile fetch calls
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` in the channels page do not set a deadline on their fetch calls. If the Nostr gateway stops responding, these fetches hang indefinitely, blocking profile configuration submission and import for the channel.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to both fetch calls. When the gateway does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects, and the caller propagates the error — the UI can then surface the failure to the user rather than silently hanging.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `NOSTR_PROFILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to each of the two existing `fetch()` calls in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to background network fetches. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Error path (rejected fetch → thrown in async function) already exists.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Stalled Nostr gateway profile PUT/POST requests now abort after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely, allowing the caller to surface the error.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation, vitest with jsdom environment). The test uses fake timers for deterministic timeout verification without real wall-clock delay.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` — unit test covering timeout behavior for both functions (passed 4/4). The test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` to control the AbortSignal.timeout timer and a mock fetch that never resolves, verifying the deadline abort fires at exactly 15 seconds.

**After-fix evidence**: Test output confirms `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` is passed to both fetch calls and stalled fetches abort cleanly after the deadline. The verify.log recording shows the full test run with `Test Files 1 passed (1), Tests 4 passed (4)` and COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0.

**Observed result after the fix**: All 4 test cases pass — signal presence verified for both functions, timeout rejection verified for both functions. Without the fix, the same tests would either deadlock or produce no timeout protection.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end test with a genuinely hanging Nostr gateway is not practical in CI for this type of fix. The unit tests verify the timeout contract at the function level using vitest fake timers, which is the standard approach used across the codebase for timeout behavior testing. Gateway failover behavior is not covered by these unit tests and is assumed correct from the existing error handling paths.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` → exit 0, 4 passed
- Test 1 (putNostrProfile): verifies `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` is passed to the fetch call
- Test 2 (putNostrProfile): verifies a stalled fetch aborts after the deadline
- Test 3 (importNostrProfile): same verification for the import function
- Test 4 (importNostrProfile): same timeout verification for the import function

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal mechanism change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.body:
Closes #106839
Related: #86761

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents running on the Claude CLI runtime with subscription-only auth (Claude Code OAuth, no Anthropic API key) would have every active-memory recall either fail with a billing rejection (no extra-usage balance) or **silently draw paid metered extra usage** (extra usage enabled) — while main-session turns correctly ran on plan limits through the CLI backend. Anthropic routing direct anthropic-messages calls on subscription tokens to extra-usage billing is long-standing behavior; the embedded runner's direct-API passthrough (`cli_runtime_passthrough_openclaw`) was never a viable path for these credentials.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an opt-in `RunEmbeddedAgentParams.cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"`: when the run's provider is `claude-cli` — directly or via a canonical `anthropic/<model>` ref whose configured `agentRuntime` is claude-cli — a backend is registered, and the ordered credential selection resolves to subscription (oauth/token) or nothing rather than an API key, the run executes through `runCliAgent` as a one-shot turn. Active-memory recall opts in. The dispatch preserves the embedded run's contracts:

- **Tool restriction is enforced server-side**: `toolsAllow` maps to the selectable-backend surface, bounds the loopback MCP grant (tools outside it can be neither listed nor called, even under bypass permission modes), and restricted runs get an exclusive loopback-only MCP bundle — user/plugin MCP servers are not merged in.
- **Transcript parity**: the run is mirrored into the caller-owned session file (user turn, live tool call/result records, assistant snapshot — flushed immediately on abort), so `persistTranscripts`, timeout partial-text salvage, and the live terminal-search watcher work identically to embedded runs.
- **Isolation**: fresh CLI process per run, no live-session reuse, session-scoped MCP cleanup (never the process-wide loopback server), CLI session bindings dropped from the result.
- **Scope**: claude-cli only; `google-gemini-cli` and custom backends keep the passthrough — their direct-API contracts were not verified and this PR makes no claims about them. An available API key keeps the existing fast passthrough. The core-side provider set could move to a `CliBackendConfig` capability flag if maintainers prefer that seam.

## User Impact

Subscription-only Claude CLI deployments get working active-memory recall on plan limits, consistent with their main turns — instead of failing every turn or silently consuming paid extra usage. Setups with an Anthropic API key see no behavior change. No config changes required; note that CLI-dispatched recalls measured 13.8–16.9s on a dev laptop, so the plugin's default 15s `timeoutMs` is tight — 30s is comfortable.

## Evidence

**Current-head success (read this first):** on PR head `cddf828336` (rebased onto main `c421a3b2e6`, dist rebuilt from that exact SHA), a live subscription-only recall with the **default plugin config** (no `timeoutMs` override) completes end-to-end:
